name: Pure-power theorem (the dominant balance at a pole is w^(K) = lambda*w^n and nothing else)
label: agent-proof
statement: Let K >= 3 and n >= 2 be integers, lambda != 0, and let Psi be a polynomial. Consider the equation w^(K) = lambda*w^n + Psi(w, w', ..., w^(K-1)). Put p = K/(n-1), give the derivative w^(j) the weight p + j and a differential monomial the sum of the weights of its factors. Assume (H): every differential monomial of Psi has weight less than n*p. Then every solution meromorphic in C is rational or W-meromorphic (elliptic, or R(exp(a*z)) with a rational function R and a != 0). If p is not an integer, the only meromorphic solutions are constants.

If p is not an integer, the only meromorphic solutions are constants.' name: Eremenko's theorem (finiteness property and one monomial of top degree)
label: published
statement: Consider an autonomous algebraic differential equation sum a_j w^j0 (w')^j1 ... (w^(k))^jk = 0 with constant coefficients a_j; the degree of a monomial is j0 + ... + jk. Suppose that the equation has the finiteness property: it is satisfied by only finitely many formal Laurent series w = sum_{k >= m} c_k z^k with m < 0, c_m != 0 — say N of them. If in addition the equation has only one monomial of top degree, then all meromorphic solutions belong to the class W (rational functions of z, rational functions of exp(a*z), elliptic functions). Each solution is either (a) elliptic with at most N poles per parallelogram of periods, or (b) of the form R(exp(a*z)), where R is a rational function with at most N poles in C minus {0}, or (c) a rational function with at most N poles in C. The source states the theorem for any single monomial of top degree and gives the proof for the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation.
source_statement: J. Math. Phys. Anal. Geom. 2 (2006), p. 282, and arXiv:nlin/0504053v1, section 'Conclusions and generalizations' (the two texts agree): 'Theorem 2. Suppose that (6) has the finiteness property, so that the equation is satisfied by finitely many Laurent series phi_n, 1 <= n <= p, of the form (2). If in addition (6) has only one monomial of top degree, then all meromorphic solutions belong to the class W. Each solution is either a) an elliptic with at most p poles per parallelogram of periods, or b) has the form R(e^{az}), where R is a rational function with at most p poles in C^*, or c) is a rational function R with at most p poles in C.'  Class W (same paper): 'f belongs to the class W if f is a rational function of z, or a rational function of exp(az), a in C, or an elliptic function.'

(Theorem 1, top-degree monomial w^2; Theorem 2 is introduced as the generalization that the method permits, with the tools Nevanlinna theory or Wiman-Valiron theory.) name: Demina's theorems for two dominant monomials lambda*w^l*(w' - mu*w)
label: published
statement: Standing assumptions of the source (dissertation, equation (1.9)): E is irreducible and of order at least 2. Consider an autonomous algebraic differential equation whose monomials of the highest degree are exactly two and form the expression lambda*w^l*(w' - mu*w) with lambda*mu != 0 and an integer l >= 1. (i) If the equation has a transcendental meromorphic solution with finitely many poles, this solution is w = h0 + h1*exp(mu*z) with constants h0 and h1 != 0. (ii) Suppose that exactly M pairwise different formal Laurent series with a pole at z = 0 satisfy the equation (finiteness property). Then every transcendental meromorphic solution with infinitely many poles is elliptic or simply periodic of the form w = delta*{sum_j eps_j sum_{n=1..p_j} ((-1)^(n-1) a^(j)_{-n}/(n-1)!) d^(n-1)/dz^(n-1)} cot(delta*(z - z_j)) + h0 + h1*exp(mu*z), where z_1, ..., z_M are pairwise different poles in a strip of periods, eps_j is 1 or 0 according to whether the solution has poles with the j-th Laurent series, a^(j)_{-n} are the coefficients of the principal part of the j-th series; if h1 != 0, then 2*delta = q*mu*i with a positive rational number q. (iii) Without the finiteness property: a simply periodic meromorphic solution with finitely many poles in a strip of periods has the form given in (ii).
source_statement: Taken from the author's doctoral dissertation (in Russian), Section 5.2: the dominant balance (5.6) 'lambda x^l {x_t - mu x}, lambda mu != 0, l in N'; Theorem 5.1 (finitely many poles: x(t) = h0 + h1 exp[mu t], h1 != 0); Theorem 5.2 (M pairwise different Laurent series (5.11); a transcendental meromorphic solution with infinitely many poles is elliptic or simply periodic of the form (5.12); if h1 != 0 there is q in Q, q > 0, with 2 delta = q mu i); Theorem 5.3 (a simply periodic solution with finitely many poles in a strip of periods has the form (5.12)). The proof of Theorem 5.2 states that the solution 'cannot have more than M different poles in a strip of periods'. The dissertation says (p. 298) that for one dominant monomial the corresponding result is Eremenko's and that 'an analogous theorem holds' for the two dominant monomials lambda x^l{x_t - mu x}.

name: One pole orbit (pure power with linear lower terms)
label: preprint
statement: Let n >= 2 and let P be a monic polynomial of degree K >= 3 with complex coefficients. Every nonconstant solution w of P(D)w + w^n/n = 0 (D = d/dz) that is meromorphic in C has exactly one pole modulo its twisted periods: if z0 is a pole, the set of all poles is z0 + Gamma, where Gamma is the group of numbers g with w(z + g) = chi(g)*w(z), chi(g)^(n-1) = 1. With m = n - 1 and p = K/m, after the translation that moves z0 to 0 the solution has one of the forms: (i) Gamma = {0} and w is a polynomial of degree p in 1/z without constant term; (ii) Gamma = (2*pi*i/k)Z, k != 0, and w = beta + sum_{j=0..p-1} d_j D^j g_r, g_r(z) = k*exp(r*k*z/m)/(exp(k*z) - 1), where exp(2*pi*i*r/m), 1 <= r <= m, is the multiplier under z -> z + 2*pi*i/k, d_{p-1} != 0, and beta = 0 unless r = m; (iii) Gamma is a lattice and w is an elliptic function of the second kind with poles of order p at the points of Gamma and nowhere else. In particular every such solution belongs to W, and it has at most n - 1 poles modulo its ordinary periods.
source_statement: Theorem A (One pole orbit): 'Let n >= 2 and let P have degree p >= 3. Every wave v of (1.1) has exactly one pole modulo its twisted periods: if z0 is a pole, then the set of all poles is the orbit z0 + Gamma. [forms (i)-(iii)] In particular, every wave belongs to W.'  Text after the theorem: 'So a wave has at most m = n - 1 poles modulo its ordinary periods'. Equation (1.1): P(D)v + v^n/n = 0, P monic of degree p; a wave is a nonconstant solution meromorphic in C; in the source the order is p and the pole order q.

conclusion.text: every nonconstant meromorphic solution is rational, simply periodic (a rational function of one exponential exp(a*z), a != 0) or elliptic and has exactly one pole modulo its twisted periods

name: At most two waves (pure power with linear lower terms)
label: preprint
statement: Let n >= 2 and let P be a monic polynomial of degree K >= 3. Up to translation z -> z + z0 and multiplication by a root of unity of degree n - 1, the equation P(D)w + w^n/n = 0 has at most two nonconstant solutions meromorphic in C. It has at most one unless n <= 3 and P is even (P(-rho) = P(rho)). For P(D) = D^4 - s with s != 0 it has exactly two, both for n = 2 and for n = 3.
source_statement: Theorem B (At most two waves): 'Let n >= 2 and let P have degree p >= 3. Up to translation and phase change, equation (1.1) has at most two waves. It has at most one unless n <= 3 and P is even. For P(D) = D^4 - s with s != 0 it has exactly two, both for n = 2 and for n = 3.'

name: Polynomial nonlinearity: P(D)w + N(w) = 0 with K odd or P even
label: preprint
statement: Consider P(D)w + B(w) = 0 with P monic of degree K and B(w) = w^n/n + B*(w), where B* contains only the powers w^2, ..., w^(n-1) (every equation Q(D)w + N(w) = 0 with a polynomial N of degree n >= 2 takes this form after moving a constant solution to 0, absorbing the linear term into P and scaling w). Let mu_m' be the group of roots of unity that preserve B (m' is the largest divisor of m = n - 1 such that B contains only powers w^j with j = 1 mod m'). Assume that K is odd or P is even. Then every nonconstant meromorphic solution belongs to W. With H = mu_m' if K is odd and H = mu_m' ∩ {1, -1} if P is even: two poles whose leading coefficients have ratio omega in H differ by a twisted period with multiplier omega, and the poles form at most m/|H| cosets of the group of twisted periods with multipliers in H.
source_statement: Theorem E.2 (Polynomial nonlinearity): 'Let B have the symmetry group mu_m', and assume that p is odd or P is even. Then every nonconstant meromorphic solution of (E.1) belongs to W. Put H = mu_m' if p is odd, and H = mu_m' ∩ {+-1} if P is even. Two poles whose leading coefficients have ratio omega in H differ by a twisted period with multiplier omega, and the poles form at most m/|H| cosets of Gamma_H.'  Proof, first paragraph: 'For odd p the recurrence determines the Laurent series from its leading coefficient. For even P the energy of a solution is constant, so by Lemma E.1 each leading coefficient carries at most one Laurent series among the poles of the solution.'

name: Clunie's lemma: a single top-degree monomial that is a power of w
label: published
statement: Clunie's lemma: let f be a nonrational meromorphic solution of f^n * P(z, f, f', ...) = Q(z, f, f', ...), where n is a positive integer and P, Q are polynomials in f and its derivatives with meromorphic coefficients a such that m(r, a) = S(r, f); if the total degree of Q in f and its derivatives is at most n, then m(r, P(z, f, f', ...)) = S(r, f). Consequence used on the site: if E has exactly one monomial of the largest total degree N >= 2 and this monomial is c*w0^N, then E = 0 reads w^(N-1) * (c*w) = Q with deg Q <= N - 1, so m(r, w) = S(r, w) for every transcendental meromorphic solution; hence a transcendental meromorphic solution has infinitely many poles. Equivalently: every meromorphic solution with finitely many poles is rational, and every entire solution is a polynomial.
source_statement: Conte-Ng-Wu (arXiv:1806.03177), subsection 'Step 2. Clunie's lemma': 'Lemma (Clunie's lemma). Let f(z) be a nonrational meromorphic solution of f^n P(z,f,f',...) = Q(z,f,f',...), where n is a nonzero positive integer, P and Q are polynomials in f and its derivatives with meromorphic coefficients {a_lambda | lambda in I}, such that for all lambda in I, m(r,a_lambda) = S(r,f), where I is some known index set. If the total degree of Q as a polynomial in f and its derivatives is less than or equal to n, then m(r,P(z,f,f',...)) = S(r,f).'  and, for the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky reduction: 'it follows from Clunie's lemma that m(r,P) = m(r,u) = S(r,u). By the First Main Theorem of Nevanlinna theory, one can deduce that u must have infinitely many poles if u is a transcendental meromorphic solution'.

name: Equal Laurent series at two poles give a period (identity theorem; a remark in the sources)
label: published
statement: Let w be a meromorphic solution of an autonomous algebraic differential equation. If the Laurent series of w(z1 + z) and w(z2 + z) at z = 0 coincide for two poles z1 != z2, then w(z) = w(z + z2 - z1): the difference is a period. Hence, if the Laurent series at the poles of w take at most N different forms, then w has at most N poles modulo its periods (at most N poles in C if w is not periodic), and for a given Laurent series with a pole at z = 0 there is at most one meromorphic solution with this expansion.
source_statement: Demina-Kudryashov 2011 (arXiv:1112.5445), Section 2: 'Note that if w(z) has more than N poles, then w(z) is periodic. Indeed, there exist poles z = z1, z = z2 of w(z) such that the functions w(z + z1), w(z + z2) are meromorphic solutions of equation (1) with a pole at z = 0. Thus we have the equality w(z) = w(z + z2 - z1).'  Remark 1: 'for fixed values of parameters in equation (1), if any, there may exist only one meromorphic solution (rational, simply periodic or elliptic) with a pole at z = 0 of type i, 1 <= i <= N.'  The same argument: Eremenko 2006, proof of Theorem 1.

name: Second-order equations w'' = F(w): first integral
label: published
statement: Let F be a polynomial of degree n. If the ODE has non-constant meromorphic solutions, then we have k <= 4 and its meromorphic solutions are characterized as follows: 1) for c = 0, we have k <= 3 and i) non-entire meromorphic solutions exist only for k = 2 or 3 and they are given in the Appendix [...]; ii) entire solutions exist only for k = 0 or 1 and they are given by [explicit formulas]'.

name: Finitely many values of the free Laurent coefficient (pure-power class, even order)
label: agent-proof
statement: Let E = c*wK - lambda*w0^n - Psi(w0, ..., w_{K-1}) with (1) c != 0, lambda != 0 constants, n >= 2; (2) p := K/(n-1) a positive integer, the weight of w_j being p + j; (3) (H): every monomial of Psi has weight < n*p; (4) K even, K >= 4. Let E_i = w^i (1 <= i <= n-1), E_n = w*w'' - ((p+1)/p)*w'^2, and let Theta = sum_i l_i(D) E_i / D^s be the differential polynomial built from the principal parts of the E_i on the formal Laurent families (the l_i are the signed maximal minors of the matrix of those principal parts; its coefficients do not contain the leading coefficient a0). For a leading coefficient a0 and a number h let w(x; h) be the formal series with free coefficient h at the Fuchs index k0 = K + 2p, and gamma_{a0,j}(h) = [x^j] Theta[w(x; h)]. Then: (A) Theta is pole-free on every family, for every a0 and every value of the parameters (whether or not the compatibility condition holds). statement: Let E(w0, ..., wK) be a polynomial with constant complex coefficients, n >= 1 its total degree, E_n its homogeneous part of degree n, tau(t) = E_n(1, t, ..., t^K) = sum_kappa b_kappa t^kappa (b_kappa = the sum of the coefficients of the monomials of E_n with kappa differentiations), and s_lo, s_hi the smallest and the largest number of differentiations of a monomial of E_n. statement: For a nonconstant w of class W let X be its model (the torus C/Lambda for the full period lattice; the sphere of s = exp(nu z) with 2*pi*i/nu primitive; the sphere of z), m the degree of w on X, and C its configuration: the poles in a period with their orders p_i and Laurent series, and the growth orders at the ends. (Lemma 2) Hypothesis (L): every Laurent expansion of a solution at a pole of a type of C is the general formal series of that type for some values of the free coefficients satisfying the compatibility conditions. If E = 0 has a solution of class W with configuration C and (L) holds, the coefficients of F_w satisfy the linear conditions obtained by substituting the series; consequently, if the system of these conditions and the compatibility conditions has no solution, E = 0 has no solution of class W with configuration C.
